newsitem.title: UK: Sears breaks itself up, Strong quits.
newsitem.headline: Sears breaks itself up, Strong quits.

text.p: British stores group Sears Plc on Tuesday announced the break-up of its retail empire, including the demerger of upmarket department store Selfridges, to try to improve returns for its long-suffering shareholders.
The retailer, hit by long-running problems from its shoe business, also announced the departure of its beleaguered chief executive Liam Strong.
Strong had come under attack for failing to turn around the group's performance after five years in the job.

Sears unveiled the long-awaited shake-up as it announced 1996 annual results and the sale of its Freemans mail order business to Littlewoods for 367.5 million pounds ($597 million), along with plans to hand the proceeds to shareholders.
The restructuring of Sears aims to ditch its loss-hit British Shoe Corporation (BSC), leaving women's and children's wear chains plus the demerged Selfridges, its star earner.
The announcement ended months of speculation about a break-up and the fate of Strong, whose failure to revive the business had tried the patience of institutional shareholders.
He was hired to inject new life into the far flung Sears retail empire but failed to do so despite a retail boom.
Chairman Sir Bob Reid said the restructuring would secure Sears' future.
"We've pruned the roses. When you prune the roses, you get good blooms, super growth," he told Reuters by telephone.
Sears has appointed David James as executive chairman of BSC to oversee its rationalisation.

"Company doctor" James, with a reputation for sorting out troubled firms, will look at each of the shoe businesses and see what their value is in the open market, mulling the advantages of holding on to them or selling them.

Reid said it was too early to say what the cost might be to Sears of the rationalisation, commenting: "We would deal with the provisions when we've actually gone through the shoe businesses one by one."
He declined to make any predictions on job cuts which might follow the restructuring.

He said Sears wanted to complete the rationalisation by the end of this year. There were several companies interested in BSC, he said, including U.S. shoe retailers Nine West Group and Payless Shoesource.
Reid said the Selfridges demerger would go ahead towards the middle of next year and described recent estimates valuing Selfridges at around 600 million pounds as conservative.
"We're looking for a lot more than that," he told Reuters, "It's a way above 600 million."
Retail analysts said the break-up was clouded by uncertainty about the cost of ditching BSC.
They doubted whether Sears could get rid of BSC at no cost and estimated it could involve a 150 to 200 million pound hit.

Different views on the cost of exiting from BSC and the value of Selfridges and the clothing businesses accounted for a wide range of break-up valuations, ranging from 78 to 90 pence a share, they said.
Sears shares were unchanged at 77.5 pence, reflecting uncertainties about the break-up.

Some analysts said Selfridges could be worth as much as 600 million pounds, while others doubted whether a potential purchaser would want to pay this much and suggested a more conservative 500 million.
The clothing businesses, including Wallis, Warehouse and Miss Selfridge, could be worth around 400 million pounds, according to one analyst, who declined to be identified.
Analysts said valuing the rump of Sears -- womenswear plus BSC -- obviously depended on the fate of BSC. "One should assume a big negative to get out of all or part of BSC," said another analyst.
"Obviously everyone's going to hope this company doctor David James (the new head of BSC) is going to manage something better," the analyst said.
Forecasts for Sears' 1997/98 results were downgraded in the light of its mixed report on current trading. One analyst said he was cutting his to 70 million pounds from 85 million previously.
